options.a: Cleaning to remove soil/bioburden before disinfection or sterilization
options.b: Sterilizing first to kill pathogens, then cleaning the instruments afterward
options.c: Soaking in high-level disinfectant to make the instruments safe to handle
options.d: Inspecting instruments under magnification for damage and missing parts

distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the sequence: sterilant cannot penetrate soil, so cleaning must come before sterilization, not after it.
distractorExplanations.c: HLD soaking is not the first step; organic soil inactivates disinfectants, so manual or mechanical cleaning comes first.
distractorExplanations.d: Magnified inspection happens in prep and pack after cleaning; it is a quality check, not the first decontamination step.

options.a: Cloth scrub top, latex exam gloves, and a surgical mask without eye protection
options.b: Fluid-resistant gown, gloves, mask/eye protection, and appropriate footwear controls
options.c: Sterile surgical gloves, a bouffant cap, and a sterile gown as worn in the OR
options.d: Lab coat, nitrile exam gloves, and safety glasses as used in the prep and pack area

distractorExplanations.a: Omits eye/face protection and uses a non-fluid-resistant cloth top; decontam splash risk requires fluid-resistant attire and eye protection.
distractorExplanations.c: Sterile OR attire protects the patient, not the worker; decontam needs fluid-resistant, heavy-duty PPE, not sterile gloves and gowns.
distractorExplanations.d: Prep-and-pack attire does not cover splash and sharps hazards; decontam requires fluid-resistant gowns, utility gloves and face protection.

options.a: Above the water line under running tap water so soil is visible
options.b: Using steel wool or abrasive pads on stainless instruments to remove stains
options.c: Below the water line to reduce aerosols, using appropriate brushes
options.d: Before soaking, using a high-pressure air gun to blow off visible soil

distractorExplanations.a: Brushing above the water line or under running water creates aerosols; scrubbing is done submerged to contain splash.
distractorExplanations.b: Abrasive pads and steel wool scratch the passivation layer and promote corrosion; use soft brushes as the IFU directs.
distractorExplanations.d: Air or water pressure guns blowing off dry soil create aerosols; manual scrubbing is done submerged first, with guns used per IFU.

options.a: Flushing with tap water only, since brushes can scratch the inner channel
options.b: Brushing with the largest brush available to maximize contact with the walls
options.c: Soaking in enzymatic solution with the ends capped to keep solution inside
options.d: Brushing and flushing according to IFU, including correct brush diameter

distractorExplanations.a: Flushing alone does not remove adherent biofilm; the IFU requires brushing with the correct-diameter brush plus flushing.
distractorExplanations.b: An oversized brush cannot pass or contact the lumen properly; brush diameter must match the channel as the IFU specifies.
distractorExplanations.c: Capping ends stops solution flow, and soaking replaces neither brushing nor flushing; lumens must be brushed and irrigated.

options.a: Break down organic soils (protein, fat, carbs)
options.b: Disinfect instruments so they are safe to handle
options.c: Dissolve rust and mineral scale on stainless steel
options.d: Work fastest in very hot water above 140 °F (60 °C)

distractorExplanations.b: Enzymes digest organic soil but are not disinfectants; instruments remain contaminated until cleaned and disinfected or sterilized.
distractorExplanations.c: Rust and scale removal needs acid or descaling products; enzymes target organic soil such as blood and protein.
distractorExplanations.d: High heat denatures the enzymes and coagulates protein; enzymatics are used in warm water at the labeled temperature.

crcst-readiness-check-decontamination-00.explanation: Follow concentration, temp, and time; rinse thoroughly to remove residues. They work only at the correct temperature and contact time.

options.a: After arrival in decontam, once the instruments are dry and easier to handle
options.b: As soon as possible at point of use, keeping instruments moist per protocol
options.c: At point of use by soaking the instruments in saline until transport
options.d: At the sterilizer, during the cycle's prevacuum conditioning phase

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting until soil dries makes it harder to remove and promotes corrosion; gross soil is removed at point of use.
distractorExplanations.c: Prolonged saline exposure causes pitting and corrosion; keep instruments moist with water-moistened towels or enzymatic spray.
distractorExplanations.d: Sterilizers do not remove soil; heat bakes on bioburden, so gross soil must be removed long before the sterilization cycle.

options.a: Sterile storage relative to the decontamination area
options.b: The prep-and-pack area relative to the corridor
options.c: The decontamination area relative to clean areas
options.d: The OR suite relative to sterile processing

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the relationship: sterile storage is kept positive so clean air flows out, while decontam is the negative room.
distractorExplanations.b: Prep and pack is a clean area kept at positive pressure; negative pressure is used to contain contaminants in decontam.
distractorExplanations.d: Operating rooms are positive-pressure spaces that protect the sterile field; in SPD the decontam area is the negative room.

options.a: Sterilize them as received, since the vendor cleaned them
options.b: Run them through IUSS just before the case to save time
options.c: Inventory them and release to the OR if the vendor seal is intact
options.d: Inspect, clean, and sterilize according to IFU before use

distractorExplanations.a: Vendor or prior-facility cleaning cannot be verified; loaners must be fully decontaminated and inspected before sterilization.
distractorExplanations.b: Immediate-use sterilization is not a substitute for complete processing of loaners, which should arrive in time for full reprocessing.
distractorExplanations.c: An intact vendor seal does not prove sterility; loaner sets are received as contaminated and processed per IFU before use.

crcst-readiness-check-decontamination-00.explanation: Loaners are high risk for inadequate processing history. Never assume loaners arrive ready for use.

options.a: Degassing, proper dilution, basket loading without overstacking, and rinsing after
options.b: Filling the tank fresh and starting immediately without degassing, then rinsing
options.c: Running hinged and dissimilar metals together closed to keep sets intact
options.d: Placing instruments on the tank floor so they get the strongest cavitation

distractorExplanations.b: Fresh solution contains dissolved gas that dampens cavitation; the tank must be degassed per the manufacturer before use.
distractorExplanations.c: Instruments must be open and dissimilar metals separated; closed boxlocks block cavitation and mixed metals cause galvanic etching.
distractorExplanations.d: Instruments must sit in a basket, not on the tank floor, which can damage both the transducer and the instruments.

options.a: Critical items that enter sterile tissue or the vascular system
options.b: Semicritical items that contact mucous membranes
options.c: Noncritical items that touch only intact skin
options.d: Implants placed during surgery when steam is unavailable

distractorExplanations.a: Critical items require sterilization under Spaulding; HLD is reserved for semicritical items such as flexible endoscopes.
distractorExplanations.c: Noncritical items such as BP cuffs need low- or intermediate-level disinfection, not high-level disinfection.
distractorExplanations.d: Implants are critical items that must be sterilized, ideally with quarantine until BI results; HLD is not acceptable.

crcst-readiness-check-decontamination-01.explanation: Critical items require sterilization; HLD is not a sterilant unless a sterilant cycle/claim applies. Per Spaulding and IFU, HLD is used when sterilization isn't feasible.

options.a: Sterilization in a short-cycle IUSS to make the set safe to handle before cleaning
options.b: Thorough cleaning/decontamination to remove soil before disinfection or sterilization
options.c: Inspection and assembly in prep and pack before the set goes through the washer
options.d: Lubricating hinged instruments with water-soluble lubricant before any rinsing

distractorExplanations.a: Sterilizing before cleaning bakes soil on and fails; IUSS still requires full cleaning first.
distractorExplanations.c: Inspection and assembly follow cleaning; sending dirty sets to prep and pack reverses the workflow and contaminates the clean area.
distractorExplanations.d: Lubrication is applied after cleaning, typically in the final rinse or at inspection, not before soil removal.

options.a: A cloth cover gown, exam gloves, and a surgical mask without goggles or face shield
options.b: Fluid-resistant attire, eye protection, and gloves appropriate to splash/sharps risk
options.c: Sterile surgical gloves and gown, since contact with contaminated instruments is brief
options.d: Hair cover, shoe covers and a lab coat, with gloves added just for sharps

distractorExplanations.a: Cloth gowns are not fluid-resistant and a mask alone leaves the eyes exposed to splash; decontam requires eye protection.
distractorExplanations.c: Sterile attire protects the patient, not the worker; decontam needs heavy-duty utility gloves and a fluid-resistant gown.
distractorExplanations.d: Gloves are required for any handling of contaminated items, not just sharps, and a lab coat is not fluid-resistant.

options.a: Flushing cools the lumen so it is not damaged by the hot washer cycle
options.b: Bioburden and debris can remain inside channels if not properly irrigated
options.c: Flushing with detergent disinfects the channel so sterilization can be shortened
options.d: Water left in the lumen helps steam penetrate during the sterilization cycle

distractorExplanations.a: Flushing is done to remove soil from channels, not to protect the device from washer temperatures.
distractorExplanations.c: Detergent flushing cleans but does not disinfect, and sterilization parameters are set by the IFU, not shortened after flushing.
distractorExplanations.d: Residual water in lumens causes wet packs and can impede sterilant contact; lumens must be dried after irrigation.

options.a: Reduce the weight of trays so they can be transported in closed carts
options.b: Prevent drying of soil that makes later cleaning more difficult and less effective
options.c: Allow the instruments to be sent directly to prep and pack, bypassing decontamination
options.d: Remove the need for enzymatic cleaning once instruments arrive in decontam

distractorExplanations.a: Transport weight is not the reason; point-of-use treatment keeps soil moist so it does not dry and harden on instruments.
distractorExplanations.c: Point-of-use treatment does not replace decontamination; every used instrument still goes through full cleaning in decontam.
distractorExplanations.d: Enzymatic or detergent cleaning is still required in decontam; point-of-use wiping removes gross soil only.

options.a: Cleanliness, function, alignment, corrosion, and completeness before packaging
options.b: Cleanliness and count only, since function is tested by the surgeon at point of use
options.c: Package integrity and chemical indicator color after the sterilization cycle
options.d: Corrosion and staining, with function checks reserved for loaner sets

distractorExplanations.b: Functional testing (scissor sharpness, jaw alignment, ratchets) is SPD's job at assembly, not the surgeon's at point of use.
distractorExplanations.c: Package and CI checks occur after sterilization; instrument inspection for soil and function must happen before packaging.
distractorExplanations.d: Function checks apply to every instrument at assembly, not just loaners; defective items are repaired or replaced.

options.a: Annual filter replacement with gasket checks done by the vendor
options.b: Intact filters/valves/gaskets and correct locking per IFU
options.c: An external CI on the lid with no internal indicator needed
options.d: Wrapping in a single layer of nonwoven wrap for extra protection

distractorExplanations.a: Disposable filters are replaced each cycle and gaskets are checked at every assembly per IFU, not annually by a vendor.
distractorExplanations.c: Containers still need an internal CI where policy or IFU requires; an external indicator shows exposure, not internal conditions.
distractorExplanations.d: Rigid containers are validated as the sterile barrier themselves; added wrapping is not required and can impair drying.

crcst-readiness-check-assembly-packaging.explanation: Containers fail if seals/filters compromised; follow load weight limits. Place internal chemical indicators as required.

options.a: Applied tightly so tape compresses the pack into a firm bundle
options.b: Oversized so extra wrap material can be tucked in several layers
options.c: Sized appropriately using sequential wrapping techniques
options.d: Folded with the final flap left loose so steam can enter

distractorExplanations.a: Over-tight wrapping strangles the pack and impedes sterilant penetration; wrap snugly without compressing contents.
distractorExplanations.b: Oversized wraps create excess layers that hinder steam penetration and drying; wrap size should match the tray.
distractorExplanations.d: A loose final flap breaks the barrier; steam penetrates through the wrap material, so every flap is secured with indicator tape.

crcst-readiness-check-assembly-packaging.explanation: Wrap integrity and technique maintain sterility barrier. Avoid tenting or strangulation of the pack.

options.a: On the outside of each package, where they replace the internal CI
options.b: At the top center of the tray, where the steam reaches the items first
options.c: On the bottom shelf over the drain, near the coolest point of the sterilizer chamber
options.d: In areas of each pack/tray challenging to sterilant penetration per policy/IFU

distractorExplanations.a: External indicators show exposure; an internal CI is still placed inside where sterilant penetration is hardest.
distractorExplanations.b: The top surface is the easiest place to reach; internal CIs go in the most challenging spot, such as the center or densest area.
distractorExplanations.c: That is where a BI process challenge device sits in the load; internal CIs go inside each pack at its hardest-to-reach point.

options.a: Ensure complete sets and document contents for OR accountability
options.b: Record the sterilizer cycle number and load contents for recall tracing
options.c: Show the technician which instruments need lubrication before packing
options.d: Replace the internal chemical indicator in trays that are counted

distractorExplanations.b: Cycle and load data go on the load sticker and sterilizer record; the count sheet lists tray contents for completeness.
distractorExplanations.c: Lubrication follows IFU and inspection checks, not the count sheet, which lists instruments to confirm completeness.
distractorExplanations.d: Count sheets are documentation, not process indicators; every tray still needs its internal chemical indicator.

options.a: Lumens capped at both ends to keep sterilant inside the channel
options.b: Moisture/residual water controls and lumen accessories per sterilizer IFU
options.c: Lumens left filled with water so steam can form inside them during the cycle
options.d: Lubricant instilled into the channel to protect it from heat damage

distractorExplanations.a: Caps or plugs block sterilant contact in lumens; channels must be open so steam or gas can enter per IFU.
distractorExplanations.c: Water left in lumens causes wet packs and blocks low-temperature sterilants; lumens are dried before packaging.
distractorExplanations.d: Oil-based lubricants inside lumens block sterilant contact; water-soluble instrument lubricant is used on hinges per IFU.

options.a: Seal instrument tips so the sterilant cannot corrode the cutting edges
options.b: Serve as a substitute for a peel pouch when sterilizing single delicate instruments
options.c: Protect sharp/delicate tips and may aid sterilant contact if designed permeable
options.d: Hold hinged instruments locked closed to prevent jaw misalignment

distractorExplanations.a: Tip protectors must allow sterilant contact; airtight sealing would prevent sterilization of the protected tip.
distractorExplanations.b: A tip guard is not a sterile barrier; the instrument still needs a validated package such as a pouch or wrap.
distractorExplanations.d: Hinged instruments are sterilized open or unlocked; stringers and racks hold them, not tip protectors.

options.a: Chemical indicators that change color before the cycle ends
options.b: Shorter exposure times because metal holds more heat
options.c: Overpressure alarms that abort the sterilization cycle
options.d: Wet packs, poor drying, and sterilization failures

distractorExplanations.a: CIs respond to process conditions, not tray weight; overweight trays condense more steam and cause wet packs.
distractorExplanations.b: Heavy metal mass acts as a heat sink and slows heat-up; it does not shorten the required exposure time.
distractorExplanations.c: Tray mass does not raise chamber pressure; the real risk is excess condensate leading to wet packs and failures.

options.a: Cleaner/positive relative to decontamination, controlled for lint/dust
options.b: Negative relative to decontamination so dust is pulled out of the room
options.c: Kept at the same pressure as decontam, with doors left open for flow
options.d: Kept above 75% relative humidity to keep lint from floating

distractorExplanations.b: A negative clean area would draw contaminated air in from decontam; prep and pack must be positive to dirty areas.
distractorExplanations.c: Neutral pressure with open doors lets contaminated air migrate; clean areas are positive and doors stay closed.
distractorExplanations.d: AAMI ST79 limits relative humidity in prep and pack to 60% or less; high humidity promotes microbial growth.

options.a: Noted on the tray tag and sent to the OR, where staff can substitute
options.b: Documented and resolved before sterilization/OR delivery per policy
options.c: Replaced with a matching instrument pulled from another assembled set
options.d: Reported only if the missing item is a sharp or a count item

distractorExplanations.a: Sending an incomplete set shifts the problem to the OR; missing items are resolved in SPD before sterilization per policy.
distractorExplanations.c: Robbing another set creates a second incomplete tray; replacements come from processed stock and are documented.
distractorExplanations.d: Every missing instrument is documented and resolved, not just counted sharps; incomplete sets delay surgery.

options.a: In decontamination, before items enter the washer-disinfector
options.b: During assembly, before packaging for sterilization
options.c: After sterilization, when the set is opened in the OR
options.d: At the sterilizer, while the load is cooling on the cart

distractorExplanations.a: Pre-cleaning checks in decontam cannot confirm cleanliness; final cleanliness and function inspection happens at assembly.
distractorExplanations.c: OR inspection is a final check; finding soil or defects there means the SPD inspection at assembly failed.
distractorExplanations.d: Inspection after sterilization would require reopening packs; function and cleanliness checks happen before packaging.

options.a: Closed on the first ratchet to protect the jaws from damage
options.b: In the open or unlocked position to allow sterilant contact
options.c: Fully locked on stringers so they do not shift during transport
options.d: Closed inside a peel pouch so the tips do not puncture it

distractorExplanations.a: Even one ratchet click blocks sterilant at the box lock and stresses the joint; hinges stay open or unlocked.
distractorExplanations.c: Stringers hold instruments open, not locked; locked boxlocks prevent sterilant contact with mating surfaces.
distractorExplanations.d: Hinged instruments in pouches are still placed open or unlocked; tip protectors are what prevent punctures.

options.a: That the load passed the biological spore challenge
options.b: That sterilant conditions were met at the indicator location
options.c: That the pack was exposed to the sterilizer, from the outside
options.d: That the sterilizer passed its daily air removal test

distractorExplanations.a: Spore lethality is verified by a biological indicator; a CI shows that process conditions reached its location.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes an external process indicator (Type 1); internal CIs show conditions met inside the pack.
distractorExplanations.d: Air removal is checked with a Bowie-Dick test in an empty chamber, not by chemical indicators inside packs.

crcst-readiness-check-assembly-packaging.explanation: CIs monitor critical process parameters; BIs are needed for lethality verification. A CI shows process conditions, not sterility by itself.

options.a: Record the sterilizer load number for recall and traceability
options.b: Verify completeness of instrument sets during assembly and at point of use
options.c: Replace the internal chemical indicator when trays are counted twice at assembly
options.d: Document instrument repair history for preventive maintenance

distractorExplanations.a: Load numbers are on the load label and sterilizer log; count sheets list set contents for completeness checks.
distractorExplanations.c: Count sheets do not monitor sterilization; trays still require internal chemical indicators.
distractorExplanations.d: Repair history lives in instrument tracking records; the count sheet confirms what belongs in the tray.

options.a: Spore kill at the coldest point of a fully loaded chamber
options.b: Air removal effectiveness / air leaks in dynamic-air-removal systems
options.c: Whether exposure time and temperature were met in each pack
options.d: Residual moisture and wet packs at the end of gravity-displacement cycles

distractorExplanations.a: Spore kill is measured with a BI in a process challenge device; Bowie-Dick tests air removal in an empty chamber.
distractorExplanations.c: Internal CIs show pack-level parameters; the Bowie-Dick test runs in an empty chamber to detect residual air.
distractorExplanations.d: Bowie-Dick is used in prevacuum sterilizers, not gravity cycles, and it detects air removal failure, not wet packs.

options.a: Ethylene oxide sterilization cycles
options.b: Dry heat sterilization cycles
options.c: Steam sterilization biological indicators
options.d: Ionizing radiation used by device manufacturers

distractorExplanations.a: EO cycles are monitored with Bacillus atrophaeus spores, not Geobacillus stearothermophilus.
distractorExplanations.b: Dry heat is also monitored with Bacillus atrophaeus spores; G. stearothermophilus is the steam indicator organism.
distractorExplanations.d: Industrial radiation historically used Bacillus pumilus as its indicator organism, not G. stearothermophilus.

options.a: Sterile once it has cooled for 30 minutes on the cart
options.b: Sterile if the internal chemical indicator inside the pack changed fully
options.c: Usable once it is dried in a warming cabinet before issue to the OR
options.d: Contaminated / not sterile for use; reprocess after investigating cause

distractorExplanations.a: Cooling does not restore the barrier; moisture wicks microbes through the wrap, so the pack is not sterile.
distractorExplanations.b: A passing CI shows conditions were met but does not cancel the contamination risk from a wet barrier.
distractorExplanations.c: Drying a wet pack afterward does not make it sterile; it must be reprocessed and the cause investigated.

options.a: Devices are heat/moisture sensitive and IFU specifies EO, with aeration afterward
options.b: Heat-sensitive items are needed right away, so the aeration phase can safely be skipped
options.c: Stainless steel sets need a faster turnaround than steam provides
options.d: Items are packaged in linen wraps that cannot tolerate steam heat

distractorExplanations.b: EO residuals are toxic to patients and staff; aeration per IFU is required before use, even for urgent cases.
distractorExplanations.c: EO cycles plus aeration take many hours; heat-stable stainless steel should be steam sterilized.
distractorExplanations.d: Linen and cellulose wraps tolerate steam; EO is selected based on device heat/moisture sensitivity and IFU.

options.a: Linen-wrapped packs and other cellulose-containing items
options.b: Heat-sensitive devices compatible with the sterilizer IFU
options.c: Liquids, powders, and oils that cannot be steam sterilized
options.d: Long narrow-lumen devices of any length or diameter

distractorExplanations.a: Cellulose (linen, paper) absorbs hydrogen peroxide and aborts or fails the cycle; use polypropylene wraps or Tyvek pouches.
distractorExplanations.c: Liquids, powders and oils are incompatible with hydrogen peroxide systems; they block or absorb the sterilant.
distractorExplanations.d: Hydrogen peroxide systems have validated lumen length and diameter limits; devices outside them cannot be processed.

options.a: Patient name and medical record number printed on every load label
options.b: Sterilizer printout of time and temperature, discarded once the BI result is read
options.c: Cycle parameters, CI/BI results, load contents, and operator identification
options.d: Monthly summaries of BI results instead of individual load records

distractorExplanations.a: Load records use lot and load numbers linked to patients through the case record; printing PHI on labels breaches privacy.
distractorExplanations.b: Printouts are part of the permanent load record and are retained per policy, not discarded after the BI result.
distractorExplanations.d: Each load needs its own record (contents, parameters, CI/BI, operator); monthly summaries cannot support a recall.

crcst-readiness-check-sterilization-007.explanation: Traceability supports recalls and accreditation. Keep records per facility policy.

options.a: Released once the Type 5 integrator passes
options.b: Sterilized using an IUSS cycle for speed
options.c: Released when the Bowie-Dick test passes
options.d: Quarantined until BI results are known

distractorExplanations.a: AAMI permits early release on a Type 5 integrator only in documented emergencies; routine implant loads await the BI.
distractorExplanations.b: IUSS is not recommended for implants; implant loads are processed in a full cycle with BI monitoring and quarantine.
distractorExplanations.c: Bowie-Dick tests air removal in an empty chamber; it does not verify spore kill in an implant load.

crcst-readiness-check-sterilization-008.explanation: Implants are high risk—await BI before release when feasible. CDC and AAMI recommend quarantine when possible.

options.a: Mechanical vacuum pulses that pull air out of the chamber before steam enters
options.b: Steam entering and forcing cooler air out through a drain passively
options.c: Steam flush and pressure pulses above atmospheric pressure
options.d: Heating the chamber dry first so air expands and vents out

distractorExplanations.a: Vacuum pulses describe dynamic-air-removal (prevacuum) sterilizers, not gravity displacement.
distractorExplanations.c: Steam-flush pressure-pulse is a separate dynamic air-removal design, not passive gravity displacement.
distractorExplanations.d: Gravity sterilizers do not preheat dry; heavier, cooler air is pushed down and out the drain by incoming steam.

options.a: Chamber pressure alone, since pressure kills microbes
options.b: Time, temperature, and saturated steam contact
options.c: Superheated dry steam at the highest possible temperature
options.d: Cycle length and the number of chemical indicators used

distractorExplanations.a: Pressure is a means to raise steam temperature; microbial kill comes from time at temperature with steam contact.
distractorExplanations.c: Superheated steam behaves like dry heat and sterilizes poorly; saturated steam with proper moisture is required.
distractorExplanations.d: Indicators monitor the process but do not make it effective; efficacy depends on time, temperature and steam contact.

crcst-readiness-check-sterilization-011.explanation: Steam sterilization requires adequate sterilant contact under validated parameters. Proper air removal and drying are also part of the designed cycle.

options.a: Confirm adequate air removal in a prevacuum sterilizer each morning
options.b: Challenge the sterilization process with resistant spores to verify lethality
options.c: Show that a package was exposed to the sterilization process
options.d: Verify that the cleaning process removed protein residue before instruments are packaged

distractorExplanations.a: Daily air-removal testing is the Bowie-Dick test; BIs use resistant spores to verify the process killed microbes.
distractorExplanations.c: Exposure is shown by an external chemical indicator; a BI challenges lethality with live spores.
distractorExplanations.d: Cleaning verification uses protein or ATP tests; BIs challenge the sterilization process, not cleaning.

options.a: Used for routine loaner sets that arrive too late for full processing
options.b: Limited to urgent situations with documented justification and proper cleaning
options.c: Used for implants when a Class 5 integrator is placed with the load
options.d: Performed with an abbreviated cleaning step because the instrument is needed now

distractorExplanations.a: Late loaners are a scheduling problem; IUSS should not be used routinely to compensate for late arrivals or low inventory.
distractorExplanations.c: Implants should not be IUSS-processed except in a documented emergency, and an integrator does not replace BI monitoring.
distractorExplanations.d: Urgency does not shorten cleaning; IUSS items need the same thorough cleaning as any other instrument.

crcst-readiness-check-sterilization-013.explanation: IUSS is for immediate need after proper cleaning—not a substitute for routine processing. Cleaning must be completed first.

options.a: Items that are heat- and moisture-sensitive when validated for EO
options.b: Stainless steel bowls and basins that need a faster turnaround than steam
options.c: Liquids and gels that cannot be placed in a steam cycle
options.d: Linen packs that must be ready for the OR within one hour

distractorExplanations.b: Heat-stable stainless items should be steam sterilized; EO plus aeration is far slower than steam.
distractorExplanations.c: EO cannot sterilize liquids; it is a gas that must contact dry, accessible surfaces.
distractorExplanations.d: EO requires long cycles plus hours of aeration, so it cannot meet a one-hour turnaround and suits heat-sensitive devices.

options.a: Moisture can create a pathway for contamination
options.b: Moisture shows the steam was superheated during exposure
options.c: Water dissolves the chemical indicator ink inside the pack
options.d: The pack must cool for an extra hour before it can be used

distractorExplanations.b: Superheated steam is too dry; wet packs result from excess condensate, wet steam, or poor loading and drying.
distractorExplanations.c: CI inks are designed for steam exposure; the concern is microbial wicking through the wet barrier.
distractorExplanations.d: Extra cooling does not fix a wet pack; it is considered contaminated and must be reprocessed.

crcst-readiness-check-sterilization-015.explanation: Wet packs compromise sterility assurance and require investigation per policy. It also indicates a process or packaging problem.

options.a: Clean, dry, well-ventilated, above the floor, away from sinks/windows moisture
options.b: Closed cabinets or open wire shelving with the bottom shelf resting on the floor
options.c: Kept above 75% relative humidity to prevent packages from drying out
options.d: Next to the sterilizer unload area so warm packs can finish drying

distractorExplanations.b: The bottom shelf must be solid and raised 8–10 inches off the floor to protect packs from floor-cleaning splash.
distractorExplanations.c: Sterile storage humidity should not exceed 60%; high humidity can compromise packaging and promote growth.
distractorExplanations.d: Packs must be cool and dry before storage; storage is separate from unloading and packs are not dried on shelves.

options.a: LIFO (last in, first out) so the freshest packs reach the OR
options.b: FIFO (first in, first out) so older sterile packs are used first
options.c: Rotation by tray weight so heavier sets are used before lighter ones
options.d: Rotation by surgeon preference so frequently used sets stay in front

distractorExplanations.a: LIFO leaves older packs at the back to outdate or be damaged; sterile stock rotates first in, first out.
distractorExplanations.c: Weight has no bearing on stock rotation; date or lot order (FIFO) determines which packs are used first.
distractorExplanations.d: Preference-based placement ignores dating; FIFO ensures older sterile items are used before newer ones.

options.a: The load sticker and expiration date, with the wrap checked at opening
options.b: The internal chemical indicator, by opening a corner of the wrap
options.c: Integrity of packaging, dryness, indicator response, and expiration/event status
options.d: The BI result for the load, which must be read before any pack is issued to the OR

distractorExplanations.a: Package integrity and dryness are checked before issue, not deferred to opening; the load label alone is insufficient.
distractorExplanations.b: Opening a pack to see the internal CI breaks sterility; the internal CI is read by the scrub person at point of use.
distractorExplanations.d: Routine non-implant loads are released without waiting for the BI; staff check integrity, dryness, CI and dating.

options.a: Aseptically transferred and used immediately—not stored
options.b: Placed in sterile storage until the end of the surgeon's day
options.c: Wrapped in a sterile towel and stored for the next case
options.d: Held on the cart until the biological indicator reads negative

distractorExplanations.b: IUSS items are not stored for later use; they are transported aseptically and used for the case at hand.
distractorExplanations.c: Wrapping after IUSS does not create a validated sterile package; IUSS items are used immediately.
distractorExplanations.d: IUSS items are needed immediately and are not held for BI results; that quarantine practice applies to implant loads.

options.a: Recording load numbers only for loaner sets, since they carry the highest infection risk
options.b: Tracking loaners, implants, and sterilization lot information for traceability
options.c: Keeping BI logs until the next accreditation survey, then shredding them
options.d: Matching sterile packs to patients through the surgeon's preference card

distractorExplanations.a: Every load needs lot/load tracking so any item can be recalled; limiting it to loaners leaves other sets untraceable.
distractorExplanations.c: Sterilization records are retained per facility policy and regulation, often several years, not until the next survey.
distractorExplanations.d: Preference cards list items a surgeon wants; patient traceability comes from load numbers recorded in the case record.

options.a: The sterilization method, with steam packs expiring after 30 days
options.b: The type of chemical indicator used inside the package
options.c: Storage conditions and package integrity or facility dating policy
options.d: The sterilizer cycle length, since longer cycles last longer

distractorExplanations.a: No fixed 30-day steam expiry applies; shelf life depends on events and storage conditions per facility policy.
distractorExplanations.b: The CI class shows how conditions were monitored; it does not determine how long the pack stays sterile.
distractorExplanations.d: Cycle length is set for lethality; once sterile, shelf life is governed by events and storage conditions.

options.a: Use it if the outer wrap shows no tears
options.b: Remove the outer wrap and use the inner pack
options.c: Wipe it down and return it to sterile storage
options.d: Consider it contaminated and reprocess

distractorExplanations.a: Floor impact can force contaminated air through the wrap and cause unseen damage; an intact look does not clear it.
distractorExplanations.b: Both wrap layers of a sequentially wrapped pack form one barrier; a dropped pack is contaminated, not unwrapped and used.
distractorExplanations.c: Wiping the exterior cannot reverse contamination from floor contact; the item is reprocessed.

crcst-readiness-check-storage-distributi.explanation: Floor contact contaminates wraps; rigid containers have specific IFU exceptions sometimes. A validated rigid container IFU may specify exceptions.

options.a: Enough stock for procedures without overstocking
options.b: Minimum stock with IUSS used to cover any shortages during the day
options.c: Maximum stock to cover a full month of cases without reorders
options.d: Stock levels set by sterilizer capacity rather than case volume

distractorExplanations.b: Relying on IUSS to cover understock is discouraged; PAR levels should meet demand without routine IUSS.
distractorExplanations.c: Overstocking crowds shelves and increases handling damage and outdates; PAR levels balance demand and space.
distractorExplanations.d: Inventory is based on procedure demand (PAR levels), not on how many loads the sterilizers can run.

crcst-readiness-check-storage-distributi.explanation: PAR levels and case cart systems improve OR support. Overstocking leads to damage and outdates.

options.a: A package in sterile storage reaches its event-related expiration date
options.b: BI failure or other sterilizer malfunction potentially affects released items
options.c: A surgeon reports a dull scissor in a tray opened in the OR
options.d: The weekly BI from the same sterilizer reads negative as expected

distractorExplanations.a: An expired or compromised package is pulled and reprocessed individually; a recall addresses a load-wide process failure.
distractorExplanations.c: A dull instrument is a repair and inspection issue, not evidence of sterilization failure needing a load recall.
distractorExplanations.d: A negative BI means no spore growth (a pass); recalls are triggered by positive BIs or other sterilizer malfunction.

options.a: Kept at high humidity so packages do not become brittle and tear
options.b: Clean, dry, well-ventilated, and protected from traffic contamination
options.c: Located beside the decontam pass-through for quick restocking
options.d: Open-access to all staff so the OR can pick its own supplies

distractorExplanations.a: Humidity in sterile storage should stay at or below 60%; high humidity wets packaging and supports growth.
distractorExplanations.c: Sterile storage is separated from decontam and kept positive; proximity to soiled areas risks contamination.
distractorExplanations.d: Sterile storage has limited access for trained staff to reduce traffic and handling damage to packages.

options.a: The fixed expiration date printed on the label is reached
options.b: An event compromises the package (eg, moisture, tears, improper handling)
options.c: The sterilizer that processed the load is next taken out of service for repair
options.d: Thirty days pass for wrapped packs and six months for pouches

distractorExplanations.a: Fixed calendar dating is time-related sterility; event-related sterility depends on package condition, not a date.
distractorExplanations.c: Equipment service does not outdate stored packages; a compromising event or facility policy does.
distractorExplanations.d: These are arbitrary time limits; event-related practice holds sterility until an event such as moisture or tearing.

crcst-readiness-check-storage-distributi.explanation: Many facilities use event-related dating; integrity events outdate the item. Facility policy governs the details.

options.a: Use open carts so OR staff can see and check the contents quickly
options.b: Use clean covered carts/containers and handle packages to protect integrity
options.c: Stack trays and peel packs together tightly to prevent shifting
options.d: Use the same cart that returns soiled instruments, wiped down between the trips

distractorExplanations.a: Open carts expose packs to dust and contact; sterile items move in covered or enclosed carts.
distractorExplanations.c: Heavy trays crush peel packs and stacking compresses wrap; packages are placed to avoid compression and punctures.
distractorExplanations.d: A cart used for soiled items must be fully cleaned (e.g., in a cart washer) before sterile use, not just wiped.

options.a: Ensure older stock is used before newer stock within dating/policy rules
options.b: Ensure newer stock is used first because it was sterilized more recently
options.c: Keep implants in date order so BI results can be skipped
options.d: Remove the need to check expiration dates when items are issued

distractorExplanations.b: That describes LIFO; FIFO rotates older stock forward so it is used before it expires or is damaged.
distractorExplanations.c: FIFO is about rotation; implant loads still require BI monitoring and quarantine whatever their shelf order.
distractorExplanations.d: FIFO reduces outdates, but staff still check dating and package integrity before issue.

options.a: Wipe it with disinfectant and return it to sterile storage
options.b: Consider it contaminated and reprocess according to facility policy
options.c: Use it if the outer wrap is dry and has no visible tears
options.d: Relabel it with a new load sticker and return it to the shelf

distractorExplanations.a: Disinfectant wiping cannot reverse contamination from floor contact; the pack must be reprocessed.
distractorExplanations.c: A dropped pack can have unseen damage, and impact can force contaminants through wrap; appearance does not clear it.
distractorExplanations.d: A new label does not reprocess the item; the contaminated pack must be unwrapped, inspected and resterilized.
